content_html:
Lenders judge how much you can borrow mainly by comparing your monthly payments with your gross monthly income. This calculator works that check backward: it starts from your income, debts and savings and finds the highest home price whose full monthly cost still fits inside the limits. The default is the classic 28/36 rule, and you can change both numbers.

The two debt-to-income ratios

  • Front-end ratio: your monthly housing cost (principal, interest, property tax, insurance, PMI and HOA dues) divided by gross monthly income. The 28/36 rule caps it at 28%.
  • Back-end ratio: housing cost plus all other monthly debt payments, divided by gross monthly income. The rule caps it at 36%.

Your housing budget is the smaller of the two limits. If you carry little other debt, the front-end limit decides. If you have car or student loan payments, the back-end limit usually takes over.

How to use this calculator

  1. Enter gross household income, the monthly payments on other debts that appear on your credit report, and the cash you have for a down payment.
  2. Enter the rate and term you expect. A higher rate reduces the price you can afford.
  3. Choose a guideline or type your own ratios. FHA's standard limits are 31% and 43%.
  4. Adjust property tax and insurance for your area. Both are entered as a yearly percentage of the price because they rise with it.

How the maximum price is found

For any price, the monthly cost is the loan payment from M = L × i / (1 − (1 + i)−n) on the price minus your down payment, plus tax, insurance and HOA dues, plus PMI if you borrow more than 80% of the price. The cost rises with the price, so the calculator searches for the highest price whose cost equals your housing budget.

A worked example

With $100,000 of income, $500 of other monthly debts and $60,000 saved, the 28% front-end limit allows $2,333.33 a month for housing, and the 36% back-end limit allows $3,000 minus $500, or $2,500. The smaller figure applies. At 6.5% for 30 years with 1.1% property tax, 0.5% insurance and 0.5% PMI, that budget supports a home of about $339,200:

Part of the paymentMonthly amount
Principal and interest on $279,200$1,764.73
Property tax$310.93
Home insurance$141.33
PMI (17.7% down)$116.33
Total$2,333.33

Under FHA's 31/43 limits the same household reaches about $370,176. If other debts were $1,000 a month instead, the back-end limit would take over and the price would fall to $300,000.

Limits of the 28/36 rule

  • It uses gross income. Taxes, retirement contributions and health premiums come out before you see your pay, so 28% of gross can be a much bigger share of take-home pay.
  • It ignores everyday costs that are not debts: childcare, commuting, utilities, food and repairs. Setting aside 1% to 2% of the home's value a year for maintenance is a common rule of thumb.
  • It is a guideline, not a lender's answer. Approval also depends on credit score, cash reserves, employment history and the lender's own rules, and automated underwriting can approve higher ratios.
  • It leaves out cash needs. Closing costs, moving costs and an emergency fund all have to come from savings beyond the down payment.
  • Loan programs differ. FHA charges mortgage insurance premiums rather than PMI, and VA loans focus on a 41% back-end ratio plus a residual income test. Enter your program's insurance rate in the PMI field for a closer estimate.

Treat the result as a ceiling. A price that leaves room in your budget is often a more comfortable target than the maximum.

faq.question: What counts as monthly debt for the back-end ratio?
faq.answer: Lenders count recurring obligations on your credit report and legal obligations, such as car loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments, personal loans, and child support or alimony. Rent you will stop paying, utilities, phone bills and insurance premiums are not counted.

faq.question: Can I get a mortgage with a debt-to-income ratio above 36%?
faq.answer: Often, yes. Many conventional loans approved through automated underwriting allow back-end ratios well above 36%, and FHA loans can go higher with strong compensating factors. A higher ratio leaves less room in your budget, so check the payment against your actual spending.

faq.question: Should I use gross or net income?
faq.answer: Lenders use gross income, which is what this calculator expects. To judge comfort for yourself, compare the monthly payment with your take-home pay as well.

faq.question: How does a bigger down payment change affordability?
faq.answer: Each extra dollar down adds about a dollar to the price you can afford, and reaching 20% down removes PMI, which frees more of the budget for the loan itself.

faq.question: Does my credit score affect how much house I can afford?
faq.answer: Yes, indirectly. A higher score usually earns a lower interest rate and cheaper PMI, which lowers the monthly cost of any given price. Try a higher and lower rate here to see how much it matters.
